name: Text Message Scams
metaTitle: Text Message Scams (Smishing): Red Flags and Examples
metaDescription: Learn how to spot text message scams (smishing), see common example patterns, and find out what to do if you clicked a suspicious link in a text.
summary: Scam texts (also called smishing) try to push you into clicking a link, calling a number, or sending money using urgency and fake alerts.
intro: Text message scams arrive as SMS or app messages that pretend to be from a delivery company, bank, government agency, or even a stranger who 'texted the wrong number.' They usually contain a short, urgent message and a link. The goal is to get you to click before you think, so you hand over login details, card numbers, or a verification code.
redFlags: An unexpected text with a link from a number you do not recognise
Urgent wording such as 'act now' or 'your account will be closed'
A request to pay a small fee to release a package or avoid a fine
Shortened or odd-looking links that do not match the real company
A request for a verification code, password, or card number

faqs.question: How do scammers get my phone number?
faqs.answer: Numbers are often guessed at random, bought from data leaks, or collected from old sign-up forms. Receiving a scam text does not mean you were specifically targeted or that your accounts are compromised.

faqs.question: Is it safe to reply STOP to a scam text?
faqs.answer: Replying anything, including STOP, can confirm to a scammer that your number is active. For unknown suspicious texts it is usually safer to not reply, block the number, and delete the message.

faqs.question: Should I click the link just to see what it is?
faqs.answer: No. Even opening a scam link can expose information about your device or lead to a convincing fake login page. If you want to check something, visit the company's official website or app directly.

howTheyWork: The text itself is rarely the theft. Its job is to move you somewhere the sender controls: a web page built for a phone screen, a number staffed by a caller, or a longer chat on a messaging app. Sending costs almost nothing, so one wording goes out to whole blocks of numbers at once, many of them simply guessed in sequence. What comes back is a card number typed into a form, a banking login, a six-digit code read off your screen, or plain confirmation that your number is live and answered.

The clumsy ones name a bank you have never used. The convincing ones land in the same thread as genuine messages, because the sender label has been set to the short name your bank or courier uses and the phone groups them together. They ask for a trivial amount, a 1.45 redelivery fee, since the card number is worth more than the fee. After you submit the form, the page forwards you to the real company's site, so nothing feels wrong. Others carry no link at all, only a friendly 'Is this still Anna's number?' that opens a conversation lasting weeks.
whoIsTargeted: Anyone with a mobile number, because lists are bought, leaked or generated in sequence. Timing does the aiming. Toll and parking texts reach commuters, parcel texts swell before gift-giving seasons, and refund texts arrive around tax deadlines. 'Hi Mum, I dropped my phone' catches parents of students and teenagers. People reading on a small screen in a queue or on a train are least able to inspect a link.

firstSteps.title: Screenshot the thread before deleting
firstSteps.detail: Capture the sender number, the wording and the link. Your bank and your mobile network will both ask what the message said and when it arrived.

firstSteps.title: Block the card you typed in
firstSteps.detail: If card details went into the linked page, phone the number on the back of the card, ask for a replacement, and query any pending transactions.

firstSteps.title: Change the password from the real app
firstSteps.detail: Open the genuine app or type the address yourself, never the link. Change that password everywhere you reuse it and sign out other sessions if offered.

firstSteps.title: Forward the text to 7726
firstSteps.detail: Mobile networks in the UK, the US and Canada accept scam texts forwarded to 7726 free of charge. Then block the number on your handset.

extraFaqs.question: Why does a scam text show up in the same thread as my bank's real messages?
extraFaqs.answer: Phones group messages by the sender label, not by who really sent them. A criminal can set that label to the same short name your bank uses, so the fake drops into the genuine thread beneath real balance alerts. The thread proves nothing. Judge each message by what it asks you to do, and check through the bank's own app.

extraFaqs.question: I tapped the link but did not enter anything. Am I at risk?
extraFaqs.answer: The risk is usually low. Loading the page tells the sender your number is active, which can bring more texts. Close the tab and do not install anything it offered. If you accepted a download or a profile, remove it and run the phone's built-in security check. Typing nothing means no card or password was captured.

name: Email Scams
metaTitle: Email Scams (Phishing): Red Flags and Example Messages
metaDescription: Recognise phishing email scams with common red flags, example message patterns, and clear steps for what to do if you clicked a link or entered your details.
summary: Email scams (phishing) imitate companies you trust to trick you into logging in on a fake page, paying a fake invoice, or downloading an attachment.
intro: Email scams, often called phishing, are messages designed to look like they come from a company or service you use, such as a bank, retailer, or streaming service. They typically warn about a problem with your account or payment and link to a fake login page. Some carry harmful attachments or fake invoices. The sender address and links rarely match the real organisation.
redFlags: A sender address that does not match the real company domain
Generic greetings like 'Dear customer' instead of your name
Urgent claims that your account is locked, expired, or will be charged
Links that point to a different website than the one displayed
Unexpected attachments or requests to 'verify' your login or payment

faqs.question: How can I check who really sent an email?
faqs.answer: Look at the full sender address, not just the display name. Hover over links to see the real destination before clicking. When in doubt, open the company's official website or app directly instead of using links in the email.

faqs.question: Is it dangerous to open a phishing email?
faqs.answer: Simply opening most emails is low risk. The risk comes from clicking links, downloading attachments, or entering information. Avoid those actions and the email itself is usually harmless to delete.

faqs.question: What should I do with a phishing email?
faqs.answer: Do not click anything. You can report it to your email provider as phishing and to the company being impersonated, then delete it.

howTheyWork: Email gives a criminal room that a text does not: a logo, a signature block, a subject line that reads like routine admin, an attachment. Three things come out the other end. A password, typed into a copy of a sign-in page. A payment, made against an invoice or a 'renewal' you never ordered. Or a foothold on the computer, through a document that asks you to 'enable content'. Mailbox passwords are valued above the others, because whoever holds the inbox can reset almost every other account you own.

Weak attempts come from a free webmail address and greet nobody in particular. Stronger ones are sent through real services: a genuine invoice raised inside a payment platform, or a real file-sharing notice with a poisoned document behind it, so the sender address passes every check. Hardest to spot is a reply inside an existing conversation, sent from a supplier's or colleague's hijacked mailbox, quoting earlier messages, with only the bank details changed. Some contain no link, just a phone number to 'cancel the charge', which moves the fraud onto a call.
whoIsTargeted: Any address in a leaked list receives the bulk versions, but role sharpens the aim. People who pay invoices, run payroll or manage a shared inbox see tailored attempts. Timing follows the calendar of paperwork: fake tax documents in filing season, fake renewal notices as subscriptions roll over, fake solicitor emails when a house deposit is due. New starters get bogus HR and IT messages in their first weeks.

firstSteps.title: Reset the mailbox password first
firstSteps.detail: If you signed in on the linked page, change your email password from a trusted device before anything else, because that inbox can reset your other accounts.

firstSteps.title: Look for forwarding rules
firstSteps.detail: Open mail settings and search for filters or forwarding addresses you did not create. Intruders add them so copies keep flowing after the password changes.

firstSteps.title: Isolate a computer that opened attachments
firstSteps.detail: If you ran a file or enabled macros, take the machine off the network, run a full security scan, and change passwords from a different device.

firstSteps.title: Use the report phishing button
firstSteps.detail: Report the message through your mail provider, then tell colleagues or family that anything sent from your address in the past hour may not be yours.

extraFaqs.question: The email came from the company's genuine address. Can it still be fake?
extraFaqs.answer: It can. Some scams travel through the real service: a criminal opens an account with a payment or document platform and uses its own invoicing or sharing tool to email you. The address is authentic and the request is not. Others come from a real person's mailbox that has been broken into. Check the claim inside your own account, never through the message.

extraFaqs.question: Why does the scam email give a phone number instead of a link?
extraFaqs.answer: Spam filters are good at catching bad links and poor at judging a phone number. The email shows a charge you do not recognise and a line to ring to dispute it. Whoever answers asks to connect to your computer to 'process the refund'. Never ring a number printed on an invoice you did not expect. Look the company up separately.

name: Marketplace Scams
metaTitle: Marketplace Scams: Buyer and Seller Red Flags to Watch
metaDescription: Spot common Facebook Marketplace and classified scams. See example patterns from fake buyers and sellers and learn how to trade safely.
summary: Marketplace scams target buyers and sellers on platforms like Facebook Marketplace, using fake payments, overpayment tricks, and pressure to move off-platform.
intro: Marketplace scams happen on buy-and-sell platforms and classified sites. A fake buyer may send a screenshot of a 'payment' that never arrives, ask for a shipping or verification fee, or try to move the conversation to email or text. A fake seller may take a deposit for an item that does not exist. The common thread is pressure to act quickly and to step outside the platform's protections.
redFlags: A buyer or seller who wants to move the chat off the platform immediately
Payment 'screenshots' instead of money actually arriving in your account
Requests to pay or refund a fee before you receive funds
Overpayment followed by a request to send the difference back
Pressure to ship or pay before you have confirmed details

faqs.question: Why do scammers want to move off the platform?
faqs.answer: Platforms have reporting tools and some buyer or seller protections. Moving to email, text, or a messaging app removes those safeguards and makes it harder to trace the scammer.

faqs.question: Is a payment screenshot proof that I was paid?
faqs.answer: No. Screenshots can be faked or show pending transfers that never complete. Only treat a payment as real once the money has actually cleared in your own bank or platform account.

faqs.question: How can I trade more safely on marketplaces?
faqs.answer: Keep conversations and payments inside the platform, meet in safe public places for local pickup, and never send a 'fee' to release a payment.

howTheyWork: Every marketplace deal has a gap between one side paying and the other handing over, and the fraud lives in that gap. A fake buyer wants your item, or a fee from you, before real funds clear. A fake seller wants payment before you hold the goods. Contact begins normally, as an enquiry on your listing or an advert in your feed. Money leaves by whatever cannot be pulled back: a transfer marked 'friends and family', a deposit to hold the item, a courier fee, or the item itself posted to someone who later disputes delivery.

Careless attempts offer more than the asking price without a single question about the item. Better ones behave like real traders. They haggle a little, ask about scratches, agree a time, then introduce one small complication: the cousin who will collect, the courier who needs an insurance fee first, a link to 'receive payment' that opens a card form. Sellers of goods that do not exist often work from an old account they have taken over, with years of history and local friends, and photographs lifted from a sold listing in another town.
whoIsTargeted: Sellers listing for the first time, who do not yet know what the platform's own payment messages look like. Buyers chasing something scarce: sold-out tickets, a console before a gift season, a particular breed of puppy, a used car priced to go quickly. People clearing a house after a move or a bereavement, with many listings live at once and little time to question each enquiry.

firstSteps.title: Look for the money yourself
firstSteps.detail: Open your bank or payment app directly and check the balance. An email or screenshot saying funds are 'pending' until you pay a fee is not a payment.

firstSteps.title: Halt the shipment or handover
firstSteps.detail: If the parcel is with a carrier, ring them and ask for an intercept or return. If a collection is booked, cancel it until cleared funds show.

firstSteps.title: Dispute what you paid
firstSteps.detail: Tell your bank or the payment app that you paid for goods which were never supplied, and ask which dispute route applies to the method you used.

firstSteps.title: Report the listing and the user
firstSteps.detail: Use the platform's report option on both, attaching screenshots of the chat, so the account can be reviewed before it reaches the next buyer or seller.

extraFaqs.question: Is meeting in person and paying cash always safe?
extraFaqs.answer: It removes most payment tricks and brings a few of its own. Meet somewhere public in daylight and take someone with you. For expensive items, count notes slowly and check them, since counterfeit cash is passed in hurried handovers. Test electronics before money changes hands, and confirm a phone is not locked to a previous owner's account or reported lost.

extraFaqs.question: A buyer wants to send a courier with the payment. How does that trick work?
extraFaqs.answer: The buyer says a courier will collect the item and hand over the money, then sends a link to 'book' it. The page asks for your card to cover insurance or to 'receive' the funds, and those details are used to take money from you. Courier firms do not deliver cash to sellers, and nobody needs your card number to pay you.

name: Job Scams
metaTitle: Job Scams: Fake Offers and Work-From-Home Red Flags
metaDescription: Identify fake job offers and work-from-home scams. See example messages, common red flags, and what to do if you shared personal details.
summary: Job scams offer easy, high-paying or remote work to collect your personal details, charge fake fees, or recruit you into moving money.
intro: Job scams use the promise of flexible, well-paid, or remote work to draw people in. A 'recruiter' may message you out of the blue, offer a role with no real interview, and ask for personal documents, an upfront fee for equipment or training, or your bank details. Some schemes turn victims into unwitting money mules by asking them to receive and forward payments.
redFlags: A job offer with no real interview or with an interview only by text or chat app
Pay that seems far too high for very simple tasks
Requests for upfront payment for training, equipment, or a background check
A recruiter who contacts you first on WhatsApp, Telegram, or text
Requests for your bank details or to receive and forward money

faqs.question: Should a real employer ever ask me to pay them?
faqs.answer: Legitimate employers do not ask you to pay for a job, training, or equipment as a condition of being hired. A request for upfront payment is a strong warning sign.

faqs.question: Why would a job ask me to receive and send money?
faqs.answer: This is a common money-mule tactic. Moving money for an 'employer' can involve handling the proceeds of fraud, which can have serious legal consequences even if you did not realise.

faqs.question: How can I check if a job offer is real?
faqs.answer: Search for the company independently, contact it through its official website, and be cautious of roles that only communicate through chat apps and pressure you to act fast.

howTheyWork: A fake job is a way of making an odd request sound like procedure. Three things get collected. Fees, dressed up as training, a uniform, a background check, or equipment you will be 'reimbursed' for. Identity documents, gathered through an onboarding form that wants a passport scan, bank details and a tax number before any contract exists. And the use of your bank account, to receive stolen money and pass it on. Contact arrives as a message on a jobs site, a chat app, or a reply to a CV you posted publicly.

The lazy offers promise a week's wage for an hour of liking videos. Careful ones copy a real company's vacancy, borrow the name of a genuine recruiter from a professional networking profile, and hold an interview with sensible questions. An offer letter follows on headed paper. Then a cheque arrives to buy a laptop from a 'preferred vendor', with the surplus to be sent on, and it bounces days later. Task scams run differently: small real payouts for the first few tasks, then a frozen balance that you must top up with your own money to unlock.
whoIsTargeted: People who need income soon and have said so in public: recent graduates, staff made redundant, parents wanting hours around school, students in the summer break, and workers seeking sponsored roles abroad. Posting a CV on an open job board or adding an 'open to work' banner invites contact. After a large employer announces layoffs, fake recruiters work through its former staff.

firstSteps.title: Stop uploading documents
firstSteps.detail: Send nothing further to the 'onboarding' portal. Write a list of what they already hold: passport or licence scan, bank details, tax number, home address.

firstSteps.title: Leave incoming money untouched
firstSteps.detail: If a cheque or transfer from the 'employer' has reached your account, do not forward any of it. Ring your bank, explain, and follow their instructions.

firstSteps.title: Ask the real employer
firstSteps.detail: Find the company's careers page yourself and ask whether the vacancy and the recruiter exist. HR teams often already know their name is being used.

firstSteps.title: Flag the advert, keep the letter
firstSteps.detail: Report the listing or recruiter profile on the job board or chat app. Save the letter, contract and messages in case your bank or the police ask.

extraFaqs.question: They paid me for the first few tasks. Does that mean it is real?
extraFaqs.answer: Small early payouts are the cost of running the con. Once you trust the dashboard, a 'combination task' or negative balance appears and you are told to deposit your own money to continue, with a bigger commission promised. Each deposit unlocks a larger demand. An employer pays you for work. It never asks you to fund your own account first.

extraFaqs.question: I sent a passport scan to a fake recruiter. What can they do with it?
extraFaqs.answer: A scan combined with your address and date of birth can be used to attempt account openings, to pass identity checks on other platforms, or to make a later scam against you more believable. Tell the passport office if it has a route for reporting misuse, watch your credit file for applications you did not make, and treat new 'refund' contacts with suspicion.

name: Bank & Payment Scams
metaTitle: Bank & Payment Scams: Fake Alerts and Transfer Red Flags
metaDescription: Recognise fake bank alerts, payment-pending tricks, and e-transfer scams. See example patterns and steps to protect your money and accounts.
summary: Bank and payment scams impersonate your bank or a payment service to trigger panic, then push you to share codes, move money, or log in on a fake page.
intro: Bank and payment scams pretend to come from your bank, a card provider, or a payment app like PayPal. They often warn of suspicious activity, a locked account, or a pending payment, then steer you toward a fake login page or a phone call where a 'fraud agent' pressures you to move your money 'to keep it safe.' Real banks do not ask you to transfer funds to a new account or to read out one-time codes.
redFlags: A message or call claiming urgent fraud on your account
Pressure to move your money to a 'safe' or 'new' account
A request to read out a one-time passcode or verification code
A 'payment pending' notice that asks you to confirm details to release funds
Links to a login page that is not the bank's official website or app

faqs.question: Will my bank ever ask me to move money to keep it safe?
faqs.answer: No. A genuine bank will never ask you to transfer your money to another account to protect it. Anyone who tells you to do this is almost certainly a scammer.

faqs.question: Should I ever share a one-time passcode?
faqs.answer: Never share one-time passcodes or verification codes with anyone, even someone claiming to be from your bank. These codes are the key to your account and payments.

faqs.question: How do I check a suspicious bank message?
faqs.answer: Do not use the links or numbers in the message. Call your bank using the number on the back of your card or in its official app, and ask them to confirm.

howTheyWork: These scams end with you pressing the button. The criminal seldom breaks into the account. You are talked into sending a transfer, approving a prompt in your app, or reading out a code, so the bank's systems see a normal customer instruction. First contact is an alert: a text about a purchase at a retailer you never visited, a call from the 'fraud team', a request for money disguised as an incoming payment. The funds go by instant transfer to an account opened in someone else's name and are split onward within minutes.

Poor versions get basic facts wrong and name a bank you do not use. Good ones open with facts about you. The caller already has your name, address and the last digits of your card, often from a fake form you half remember filling in last week. They invite you to compare the number they are calling from with the one on your card, knowing it can be spoofed. They stay calm, warn you about fraud themselves, and explain that the warning screens in your banking app are part of the 'investigation' and should be tapped through.
whoIsTargeted: Customers who recently entered card details on a fake parcel or toll page get a call days later from a 'fraud team' holding those details. House buyers are hit at completion, when a large transfer is expected and an email with 'updated' account details fits the moment. New users of instant payment apps and anyone selling something online meet the fake-payment and accidental-transfer versions.

firstSteps.title: Hang up and redial the bank
firstSteps.detail: End the call, then use another phone or wait a few minutes before dialling the number printed on your card. Ask whether the fraud team contacted you.

firstSteps.title: Say 'I have been scammed'
firstSteps.detail: If money has left, say so plainly and give the time, amount and receiving account. Banks can sometimes reach the receiving bank while funds remain.

firstSteps.title: Freeze cards and remove new payees
firstSteps.detail: Freeze the card in your app, change the online banking password, and delete any payee or registered device that you do not recognise.

firstSteps.title: Note what the caller knew
firstSteps.detail: Write down the number displayed, the name given and each detail they quoted about you. It helps the bank's investigators and hints at where your data leaked.

extraFaqs.question: The caller knew my name, address and card digits. How is that possible?
extraFaqs.answer: Usually the details came from you at an earlier stage. A fake delivery or fine page collected your card and contact information, and the phone call is the second act. Other data comes from breached retailer databases. Knowing facts about you shows that someone holds your data. It says nothing about who employs them.

extraFaqs.question: Someone sent me money by mistake and wants it back. What should I do?
extraFaqs.answer: Do not return it yourself. The original payment may have come from a stolen card or hacked account and can later be reversed, leaving you short by whatever you sent on. Tell the sender to raise it with their own bank, and tell your bank or the payment app so the reversal is handled through official channels.

name: Delivery & Postal Scams
metaTitle: Delivery & Postal Scams: Fake Parcel Texts and Fees
metaDescription: Spot fake delivery and postal scam texts that ask for a redelivery fee or personal details. See example patterns and what to do next.
summary: Delivery scams impersonate couriers and postal services with fake 'missed delivery' or 'customs fee' messages that lead to phishing pages.
intro: Delivery and postal scams play on the fact that many people are expecting a parcel. A text or email claims a delivery failed, a small redelivery or customs fee is due, or an address needs confirming, and links to a fake page that collects card and personal details. Real couriers usually do not ask for payment by text link, and any genuine charge can be checked through the official tracking page.
redFlags: An unexpected 'missed delivery' message with a link
A request to pay a small redelivery, customs, or handling fee
Links that do not match the courier's official website
Requests for personal or card details to 'reschedule' delivery
Urgent wording warning the parcel will be returned or destroyed

faqs.question: Do couriers charge fees by text message?
faqs.answer: Genuine redelivery is normally free, and any real customs charge can be confirmed through the courier's official website. A small fee demanded through a text link is a common scam pattern.

faqs.question: I am expecting a parcel, so is the text probably real?
faqs.answer: Scammers rely on this. Even if you are expecting something, check the tracking number on the courier's official site or app rather than using the link in the message.

faqs.question: What should I do with a suspicious delivery text?
faqs.answer: Do not click the link. Verify any delivery directly with the retailer or courier, then report and delete the message.

howTheyWork: A fake delivery notice exists to collect a full card record for the price of a tiny fee. The page asks for name, address, phone number, date of birth and card, all on one form, 'to rebook'. The fee might be 1.99. Nobody wants the 1.99. Days later the card is tested with small purchases or loaded into a mobile wallet, or the whole record is handed to a caller who rings as your bank. First contact is a text or email naming a courier, sometimes a printed card through the letterbox with a QR code.

Sloppy ones name a courier that does not operate where you live. Convincing ones show a tracking number, a progress bar and a countdown to 'return to sender'. They copy a postal service's colours down to the footer, then pass you through a 'verification' step where you enter the code your bank has just texted, which approves a far larger payment or a wallet enrolment. The message never says who sent the parcel or what is in it, because the criminal has no idea. Genuine notices tend to carry the retailer's name or the tracking number from your order.
whoIsTargeted: People who order online often, which is nearly everyone in the weeks before gift-giving holidays and during big sales. Anyone waiting on goods from abroad half expects a customs charge and pays a fake one without surprise. Small businesses receiving stock daily, students expecting parcels from home, and people who have just moved and are unsure which address a sender used.

firstSteps.title: Track the parcel from your order email
firstSteps.detail: Find the tracking number in the retailer's confirmation and enter it on the courier's own site or app. If nothing is being held, the notice was fake.

firstSteps.title: Cancel the card on the form
firstSteps.detail: Freeze it in your banking app and ask the issuer for a replacement. Mention that the same form also took your address and date of birth.

firstSteps.title: Refuse wallet and payment codes
firstSteps.detail: If a code arrives to add your card to a phone wallet or approve a purchase, share it with nobody and tell the bank that it came.

firstSteps.title: Expect a fake bank call
firstSteps.detail: For the next few weeks, treat any caller from your bank's 'fraud team' as suspect. Put the phone down and ring the number on your card.

extraFaqs.question: I only paid a fee of a pound or two. Is that all I have lost?
extraFaqs.answer: Probably not. The small charge was an excuse to collect your full card details and personal information. Larger charges may follow, or the card may be added to a phone wallet somewhere else. Have the card cancelled and reissued even if only the small amount has gone, and read the next two statements line by line.

extraFaqs.question: A missed-delivery card came through my door. Could that be fake too?
extraFaqs.answer: It can be. Fake cards copy a courier's layout and give a phone number charged at a premium rate, or a QR code leading to a payment page. Do not ring or scan. Use the tracking number from your order, or ask at the local depot or post office whether anything is waiting for your address.

name: Rental & Housing Scams
metaTitle: Rental & Housing Scams: Deposit and Listing Red Flags
metaDescription: Avoid rental scams that ask for a deposit before viewing. See example patterns, common red flags, and how to verify a listing safely.
summary: Rental scams advertise homes that are not available, then pressure you to pay a deposit or holding fee before you can view the property.
intro: Rental and housing scams post attractive listings, often with photos copied from real ads, at below-market prices. The 'landlord' is usually away or abroad and asks for a deposit or first month's rent before any viewing, often by wire transfer, e-transfer, or gift card. Once the money is sent, the listing and contact disappear.
redFlags: A landlord who cannot show the property in person or by live video
A request for a deposit or holding fee before any viewing
Rent that is unusually cheap for the area
Pressure to pay quickly because of 'other interested tenants'
Payment requested by wire transfer, e-transfer, or gift card

faqs.question: Should I ever pay a deposit before seeing a rental?
faqs.answer: Avoid paying any deposit or fee before you have viewed the property and confirmed the landlord has the right to rent it. Legitimate landlords expect you to view first.

faqs.question: How can I tell if a listing is stolen?
faqs.answer: Search the listing photos and text online. If the same images appear on other sites under different names or prices, it may be a copied or fake listing.

faqs.question: What payment methods are safest for rentals?
faqs.answer: Be cautious with wire transfers, e-transfers, and gift cards, which are hard to reverse. Use traceable methods and get a signed agreement after viewing.

howTheyWork: What is being sold is access to a home the advertiser has no right to let. Either the property belongs to someone else entirely, or the 'landlord' has brief access through a holiday booking and shows it to several hopeful tenants in one weekend. First contact is your own enquiry on a listings site, answered fast and moved to email. Money leaves as a holding deposit, a month's rent in advance, or a fee for a credit check. The application form collects a passport copy, payslips and bank statements, which are sold on separately.

A weak advert gives itself away with a story about working overseas and keys to be posted after payment. The polished version includes a viewing. Someone meets you at the door, has a key or a code, and walks you round. A tenancy agreement arrives as a tidy PDF carrying an agent's logo, and you get a receipt. Missing are the two things a renter seldom checks: proof that this person owns the property or acts for the owner, and, where the law requires one, a deposit lodged with a protection scheme instead of a private account.
whoIsTargeted: People renting from a distance: students arriving for a new term, workers relocating for a job, service families posted to a new base, and anyone moving to a city where decent flats go within hours. Late summer, before term begins, is the busiest stretch. Holidaymakers booking a villa or cottage meet the same trick, with an 'owner' offering a discount for paying outside the booking site.

firstSteps.title: Report the transfer as fraud
firstSteps.detail: Ring your bank straight away with the receiving account details. The earlier it contacts the receiving bank, the more likely some of the deposit is still there.

firstSteps.title: Check who owns the address
firstSteps.detail: Search the official land or property register for your area, or ask the building's managing agent, and compare the owner's name with the person you paid.

firstSteps.title: Protect the paperwork you supplied
firstSteps.detail: If a passport copy, payslips or bank statements went with the application, tell your bank and ask the credit agencies about a fraud alert.

firstSteps.title: Get the advert taken down
firstSteps.detail: Send the listing link, the messages and your payment receipt to the listings platform, and keep copies of everything for a police report.

extraFaqs.question: I viewed the flat in person and it was still a scam. How?
extraFaqs.answer: A viewing only proves the person had a way in. Scammers book a flat as a short holiday let, or obtain a key safe code, then show people round as the 'landlord' and take several deposits for the same rooms. Ask for proof of ownership or of the agent's authority, and check it independently before paying anything.

extraFaqs.question: The landlord asked me to prove my funds by sending money to a relative. Why?
extraFaqs.answer: It is an old trick. You send the deposit to a friend or relative through a money transfer service, 'so it stays under your control', then email a photo of the receipt as proof. The details on that receipt let the scammer collect the cash using forged identification. No landlord needs to watch money move. A bank statement shows funds.

name: Social Media Scams
metaTitle: Social Media Scams: DMs, Giveaways and Account Tricks
metaDescription: Recognise social media scams including fake verification, giveaways, account recovery, and romance DMs. See example patterns and safety steps.
summary: Social media scams use DMs, fake giveaways, verification offers, and romance messages to steal logins, money, or personal information.
intro: Social media scams reach you through direct messages, comments, and fake pages on platforms like Instagram, Facebook, and TikTok. Common forms include fake 'verification' or copyright warnings that lead to phishing pages, prize giveaways that ask for a fee, account-recovery tricks that hijack your profile, and romance scams that build trust before asking for money.
redFlags: A DM warning your account will be deleted unless you 'verify' now
A message from a friend's hacked account asking for a code or help
Prize or giveaway wins that require a fee or your login to claim
A new online romance that quickly asks for money or gift cards
Links to login pages that are not the platform's official website

faqs.question: Does a platform send verification warnings by DM?
faqs.answer: Official verification and policy notices come through in-app settings or official channels, not urgent DMs with outside links. Treat such DMs as likely phishing.

faqs.question: A friend messaged asking for a code. Is that safe?
faqs.answer: If a friend asks you to share a verification code or 'help recover' their account, their account may be hacked. Never share codes, and contact your friend another way to check.

faqs.question: How do I protect my social media accounts?
faqs.answer: Turn on two-factor authentication, use a strong unique password, and be cautious with links in DMs, even from accounts you know.

howTheyWork: On social platforms the account is the prize as often as the money. A profile with years of history, friends who trust it and perhaps a business page or advertising account attached is a tool for the next hundred frauds. Contact comes as a DM, a tag in a comment, a friend request from a copy of someone you know, or a sponsored post. A stolen login is used at once. The email and phone number on the account are swapped, and your contacts start receiving requests for a 'quick favour' or tips about an investment.

Easy ones to spot come from blank profiles with a string of digits in the handle. Convincing ones come from a person you know, because their account was taken an hour ago. The message sounds like them, mentions a shared group, and asks for something small: vote for me in this contest, receive a code for me, look at this video of you. Fake 'support' accounts reply beneath your public complaint to a brand within minutes, wearing its logo and a near-identical handle, and draw you into DMs before the real team has read the post.
whoIsTargeted: People with something attached to a profile: small businesses that depend on a page, creators with a following, admins of local groups. Anyone who complains publicly about an airline, bank or retailer attracts fake support replies. Those who announce a bereavement, a fundraiser or a lost pet receive tailored approaches. Teenagers are singled out for sextortion through new 'friend' accounts that ask for photos.

firstSteps.title: Try your login straight away
firstSteps.detail: If it still works, change the password, then confirm the email address and phone number on the account are yours and remove any that are not.

firstSteps.title: End every other session
firstSteps.detail: In security settings, log out all devices and revoke connected apps you did not add. A hijacked session can outlive a password change until you end it.

firstSteps.title: Start official account recovery
firstSteps.detail: If you are locked out, use the 'hacked' or 'need more help' route in the platform's own app. Ignore offers in comments to recover it for a fee.

firstSteps.title: Warn your contacts another way
firstSteps.detail: Ask a friend to post, or message people directly, that requests for codes, votes or money from your profile today did not come from you.

extraFaqs.question: Someone offers to recover my hacked account for a fee. Should I pay?
extraFaqs.answer: No. People who reply to posts about hacked accounts with offers of 'recovery' are running a second scam on the same victims. They take a fee, ask for more, or request your email login and take that as well. Only the platform can restore an account, through the recovery process in its app or help centre, which costs nothing.

extraFaqs.question: Why would a scammer copy my profile instead of hacking it?
extraFaqs.answer: Cloning needs no password. They save your public photos, create a profile in your name, and send requests to your friends list, which is often visible to anyone. Once friends accept, the clone asks them for money or sends a link. Make your friends list private, report the copy as impersonation, and ask friends to report it too.

name: Online Shopping Scams
metaTitle: Online Shopping Scams: Fake Stores and Order Red Flags
metaDescription: Spot fake online stores and shopping scams. See common red flags, example patterns, and how to check a website before you buy.
summary: Online shopping scams use fake stores, too-good-to-be-true deals, and fake order emails to take your money or card details.
intro: Online shopping scams involve fake or dishonest stores that advertise popular products at very low prices, then take payment and deliver nothing, a counterfeit, or a cheap substitute. Related scams send fake order-confirmation or 'problem with your order' emails to harvest your login and card details. These sites often appear briefly through social media ads before disappearing.
redFlags: Prices that are far below the normal price for popular items
A brand-new store with no real reviews or contact details
Only unusual payment methods such as wire transfer or gift cards
Fake order or shipping emails for purchases you did not make
Pressure from countdown timers and 'almost sold out' messages

faqs.question: How can I check if an online store is legitimate?
faqs.answer: Look for a real contact address, search the store name with the word 'scam' or 'review', and check how long the site has existed. Be wary if only risky payment methods are offered.

faqs.question: Is it safer to pay by card than by bank transfer?
faqs.answer: Card payments often carry more consumer protection and can be disputed, while wire transfers and gift cards are very hard to reverse. Avoid stores that only accept hard-to-trace methods.

faqs.question: I got an order email for something I did not buy. What now?
faqs.answer: Do not click the links. Log in to the real retailer's website directly to check your orders, and treat the email as possible phishing.

howTheyWork: A fake shop is cheap to build. It needs a storefront template, product photos taken from a real brand, a payment form, and a few days of adverts on social feeds. Orders come in, and the site sends nothing, or posts a token item so a tracking number exists, or keeps the card details for later use. Some are subscription traps, where a 'free trial, just pay postage' checkout hides a monthly charge in pale grey text. Payment is by card when the site wants to look normal and by bank transfer when it wants no comeback.

A crude shop cuts prices to a fraction and writes in oddly translated English. The capable ones clone a real retailer's whole site at a web address one letter out, or revive the name of a closed high-street chain for a 'closing down sale'. They display trust badges, a returns policy copied word for word, and reviews hosted on their own pages. A tracking number arrives showing a parcel delivered to your town, later used to contest your refund claim. The tells are absences: no company registration, no returns address, no phone line that anyone answers.
whoIsTargeted: Shoppers hunting one specific item that is sold out everywhere or priced out of reach, in the run-up to gift seasons and sale weekends. Parents after the toy of the year. People scrolling late at night who buy from an advert without leaving the app. Anyone looking for a cheaper route to medication, software licences, flights or event tickets.

firstSteps.title: Capture the site before it vanishes
firstSteps.detail: Screenshot the web address, product page, order confirmation and emails now. Your card provider will want evidence of what was promised and the shop may disappear.

firstSteps.title: Raise a card dispute today
firstSteps.detail: Tell the provider that the goods were not supplied or the trader is fraudulent, and ask how to start a chargeback or claim. Time limits apply.

firstSteps.title: Block repeat charges from the merchant
firstSteps.detail: Check whether the checkout signed you up to a subscription. Ask the bank to stop future payments to that merchant, since trial offers often bill again.

firstSteps.title: Retire the password you gave the shop
firstSteps.detail: If you made an account there with a password used elsewhere, change it on those other sites before the shop's owners try it on them.

extraFaqs.question: Tracking says delivered but nothing arrived. What is going on?
extraFaqs.answer: Fake shops sometimes post a worthless item, or obtain a tracking number for a different parcel delivered in your postcode area. The 'delivered' status is then shown to your card provider as proof. Say exactly that in your dispute, ask the courier for the delivery address and weight recorded against the number, and include their reply.

extraFaqs.question: I received a cheap item nothing like the photos. Is that fraud or bad service?
extraFaqs.answer: When the advert showed a branded product and a trinket turned up, the goods were misdescribed, and card providers generally accept 'not as described' as grounds for a dispute. The seller will often offer a partial refund if you keep the item, or insist you post it abroad at your own cost. Keep the item and packaging as evidence.

name: Crypto & Investment Scams
metaTitle: Crypto & Investment Scams: Fake Returns and Red Flags
metaDescription: Recognise crypto and investment scams promising guaranteed or high returns. See example patterns, red flags, and how to protect your money.
summary: Crypto and investment scams promise high or guaranteed returns to lure you into fake platforms, then block withdrawals once you deposit.
intro: Crypto and investment scams advertise unusually high or 'guaranteed' returns through fake trading platforms, social media tips, or a new online contact who offers to help you invest. Early on, a fake dashboard may show profits to encourage bigger deposits. When you try to withdraw, you are asked for more fees and taxes, and eventually the platform and contact disappear with your money.
redFlags: Promises of guaranteed or unusually high returns with no risk
Pressure to invest quickly before a 'limited' opportunity ends
A new online contact who offers to manage your trades
Requests for more fees or taxes before you can withdraw
Unregistered platforms that are hard to verify or research

faqs.question: Can any investment guarantee high returns?
faqs.answer: No legitimate investment can guarantee high returns with no risk. Promises of guaranteed profits are one of the clearest signs of an investment scam.

faqs.question: Why can't I withdraw my profits?
faqs.answer: Fake platforms show paper 'profits' to keep you depositing, then demand endless fees or taxes to release funds. The money is usually already gone, and paying more will not recover it.

faqs.question: How can I check an investment platform?
faqs.answer: Verify whether the company is registered with your local financial regulator, and be cautious of anyone who contacts you first with an investment opportunity.

howTheyWork: The platform is a stage set. You see a trading screen with charts, a balance and a withdraw button, yet deposits never reach a market. They go straight to wallets the operators control, and the figures on screen are typed in by them. Contact comes from an advert with a famous face, a 'signals' group on a messaging app full of planted members posting wins, or someone met weeks ago on a dating app. Your money goes from bank to a genuine exchange, becomes crypto, and is sent to an address given in chat. That final transfer cannot be reversed.

Blunt versions promise to double your coins by Friday. Patient ones never hurry you. They suggest a small first deposit, display gains, and let you take a little out so the system looks sound. An 'account manager' phones weekly and talks soberly about risk. The site shows a licence number borrowed from a real firm with a similar name. The trap shuts only when you request a large withdrawal: a tax, an anti-money-laundering deposit, an upgrade fee, each payable from fresh funds and never deductible from the balance you supposedly hold.
whoIsTargeted: People holding a lump sum and a reason to grow it: a redundancy payment, an inheritance, a pension pot newly within reach, proceeds of a house sale. Savers tired of low interest. Newcomers to crypto during price surges, when headlines suggest everyone else is getting rich. Lonely people befriended over weeks by a new online contact. Earlier victims, approached again by 'recovery agents'.

firstSteps.title: Refuse the release fee
firstSteps.detail: Whatever tax, fee or 'unlock' payment is demanded, do not send it. A firm holding your money has no need of new money before returning it.

firstSteps.title: Copy wallet addresses and transaction hashes
firstSteps.detail: From your exchange history, record every address you sent to and each transaction ID. They are the only lasting trace of where the coins went.

firstSteps.title: Alert your bank and exchange
firstSteps.detail: Report the transfers to the bank you funded from, and give the genuine exchange the destination addresses so it can flag them and review linked accounts.

firstSteps.title: Remove apps they had you install
firstSteps.detail: Uninstall any screen-sharing or 'trading' app added at their request, change your passwords, and move remaining crypto to a fresh wallet with a new seed phrase.

extraFaqs.question: I withdrew a small amount early on. Does that prove the platform is genuine?
extraFaqs.answer: It proves the operators will spend a little to gain a lot. Letting you take out a small sum is a standard step, timed just before they suggest a bigger deposit. The real test is whether you can withdraw most of your balance to your own bank without paying anything first. Scam platforms fail that test every time.

extraFaqs.question: A firm says it can trace and recover my stolen crypto. Should I use it?
extraFaqs.answer: Be very wary. People who have lost money are contacted again, often by the same group, by 'recovery specialists' who claim to have located the funds and need an upfront fee to release them. A confirmed blockchain transfer cannot be undone by a private firm. Report the loss to the police or your national fraud reporting service, which charge nothing.

name: Government, Tax & Legal Scams
metaTitle: Government, Tax & Legal Scams: Fake Agency Red Flags
metaDescription: Recognise scams that impersonate tax, immigration, and law-enforcement agencies. See example patterns and how to verify official contact.
summary: Government and tax scams impersonate agencies to threaten fines, arrest, or deportation, then demand urgent payment by unusual methods.
intro: Government, tax, and legal scams pretend to come from a tax authority, immigration office, court, or police force. They claim you owe money, missed a payment, or face arrest or deportation, and demand immediate payment, often by gift card, wire transfer, or cryptocurrency. Real agencies communicate through official letters and channels and do not demand payment in gift cards or threaten instant arrest by phone or text.
redFlags: Threats of arrest, deportation, or legal action unless you pay now
Demands for payment by gift card, wire transfer, or cryptocurrency
Caller ID or sender details that 'spoof' a real agency
Pressure to keep the matter secret and act immediately
Requests for personal identifiers like your tax or ID number

faqs.question: Do government agencies demand payment by gift card?
faqs.answer: No legitimate agency asks for payment in gift cards, cryptocurrency, or wire transfers. This demand is a clear sign of a scam.

faqs.question: Can a tax office threaten to arrest me by phone?
faqs.answer: Genuine agencies do not threaten immediate arrest or deportation over the phone or by text. These threats are designed to scare you into paying quickly.

faqs.question: How do I verify a message from a government agency?
faqs.answer: Do not use the contact details in the message. Look up the agency's official website or phone number independently and confirm any claim directly.

howTheyWork: Authority does the work here. A tax office, a court or a police force can fine you or detain you, so a message in their name gets obeyed before it gets checked. Two shapes dominate. One is the threat: a debt, a warrant, a visa problem, to be settled today. The other is the reward: a rebate, a grant, a benefit top-up, which needs your bank details and identity number to 'process'. Contact comes by recorded call, text or email, or through a copy of an official website sitting above the real one in search adverts.

Crude calls threaten arrest within the hour. Careful versions arrive in the right month, quote a plausible reference number, and copy the layout of a genuine notice. The caller gives a badge number, offers to transfer you to a 'supervisor', and may know part of your identity number from an earlier leak. Copycat application sites are hardest to recognise, because the passport form or travel permit does eventually arrive. You have simply paid several times the official fee and handed your documents to a stranger along the way.
whoIsTargeted: Taxpayers near filing deadlines and during refund season. The self-employed, who deal with the tax office directly. Recent immigrants and international students, who fear for their status and may not know how local agencies write to people. Pensioners and those on state health cover. Drivers renewing a licence, and founders whose newly registered company has just appeared on a public register.

firstSteps.title: End the call unpaid
firstSteps.detail: Put the phone down. No genuine agency drops its claim because you hung up, and any real debt will show in your own online tax account.

firstSteps.title: Report the identity number you gave
firstSteps.detail: If you disclosed a tax, social security or national insurance number, contact the issuing agency through its official fraud route and ask what protection it offers.

firstSteps.title: Ring the gift card company
firstSteps.detail: If you bought cards and read out the codes, call the card brand at once with the receipt and card numbers, in case unspent value remains.

firstSteps.title: Sign in to the official portal
firstSteps.detail: Type the address of your tax or benefits account yourself. Check that the contact details and bank account on file have not been altered.

extraFaqs.question: I paid a website far more than expected to renew my passport. Was I scammed?
extraFaqs.answer: You probably used a copycat service. These sites advertise above the official one, look governmental, and charge heavily for forwarding a form you could have submitted directly. Some deliver and some do not. Ask the official passport office whether an application exists in your name, and ask your card provider about a dispute if the site misled you.

extraFaqs.question: Does a real tax office ever phone people?
extraFaqs.answer: Some do, in limited circumstances, and usually after writing to you about the same matter. What a genuine officer will not do is demand payment during the call by gift card, crypto or transfer to a personal account, or tell you to keep the call secret. If a call surprises you, say you will ring back, and use the number from the agency's official site.

name: Phone & Voice Scams
metaTitle: Phone & Voice Scams (Vishing): Red Flags and Examples
metaDescription: Recognise phone call and voicemail scams (vishing): robocalls, spoofed numbers, fake bank and agency calls, and voice cloning. See red flags and what to do.
summary: Phone scams (vishing) use live calls, robocalls, and voicemails to impersonate banks, agencies, and companies and pressure you into payments, codes, or remote access.
intro: Phone and voice scams reach you through live calls, automated robocalls, and voicemails. Scammers spoof real numbers to appear as your bank, a government agency, tech support, or a delivery company, then use urgency, threats, or reassurance to get you to share codes, move money, grant remote access, or call a premium number. Increasingly, they also use AI voice cloning to imitate people you know.
redFlags: An unexpected call pressuring you to act immediately
Caller ID that appears to show a bank, agency, or company
A request for one-time codes, PINs, or passwords
Instructions to move money, buy gift cards, or grant remote access
A recorded message telling you to press a key or call a number back

faqs.question: Can caller ID be faked?
faqs.answer: Yes. Scammers spoof numbers so the call appears to come from your bank or a real agency. Do not trust caller ID alone; hang up and call back on an official number.

faqs.question: Will my bank ever ask for a code over the phone?
faqs.answer: No. Banks never ask you to read out one-time codes, PINs, or full passwords. Anyone who does is a scammer, even if the call seems official.

faqs.question: How do I check a suspicious call?
faqs.answer: Hang up, wait a moment or use another phone, and call the organisation back using the number on your card, a bill, or its official website.

howTheyWork: A live call takes away your time to think, and that is what the caller is after. With a text you can pause, reread, ask someone. On the phone a confident voice fills each silence, answers every doubt as it forms, and stays with you while you walk to the computer or the shop. Calls are placed by autodiallers working through number ranges, and pressing a key or saying hello routes you to a person. What leaves is a card number read aloud, a code, a transfer made while they wait, or control of your screen.

A robotic voice announcing a prize from a draw you never entered fools few people. A calm human does better, with call-centre noise behind them, a staff ID, and a reference number they ask you to write down. They may send a text mid-call that lands in your bank's message thread as 'proof'. On some landlines they stay connected after you hang up and play a dial tone, so the call you then make to check goes straight back to them. Cloned voices of relatives add a few seconds of crying before a 'lawyer' takes over.
whoIsTargeted: Households with a landline, which tend to be older and tend to answer. People at home in working hours because they are retired, unwell or caring for someone. Grandparents, for the late-evening 'I am in trouble, please do not tell Mum' call. Anyone who recently filled in an online quote form for insurance or a loan, since those details are resold as calling lists.

firstSteps.title: Put the phone down mid-sentence
firstSteps.detail: You owe no reason and no polite ending. If they ring straight back, let it ring out. A genuine organisation will be content for you to call them.

firstSteps.title: Call back on a different line
firstSteps.detail: Use a mobile if the call came to a landline, or wait ten minutes. Dial a number you found yourself and ask whether they tried to reach you.

firstSteps.title: Undo whatever you handed over
firstSteps.detail: A card number read aloud means cancelling the card. A shared code means telling the company that issued it. Remote access means switching the computer off.

firstSteps.title: Switch on call screening
firstSteps.detail: Ask your phone provider about call blocking, or enable the handset's option to silence unknown callers, so repeat attempts over the coming days reach voicemail.

extraFaqs.question: Is it risky just to answer a call from a number I do not know?
extraFaqs.answer: Answering costs nothing in itself, though it marks your number as live and tends to attract more calls. The danger lies in what follows: staying on the line, confirming personal details, pressing keys to 'speak to an agent'. If the number is unfamiliar, let voicemail take it. Real callers leave a message you can verify in your own time.

extraFaqs.question: An overseas number rang once and stopped. Should I call it back?
extraFaqs.answer: Leave it. Single-ring calls from unfamiliar international codes are meant to make you return the call to a premium-rate line, where hold music or a recorded message keeps you connected while charges build. If you have already rung back, check your bill and tell your mobile network. Anyone who needs you will try again or leave a message.

name: Romance & Dating Scams
metaTitle: Romance & Dating Scams: Red Flags and Examples
metaDescription: Spot romance and dating scams: fake profiles, love bombing, requests for money, crypto investment lures, and sextortion. See red flags and safe steps.
summary: Romance scams build a fake relationship online to gain trust, then ask for money, gifts, or investment, or use intimate images for blackmail.
intro: Romance and dating scams begin with a fake or stolen identity on a dating app or social platform. The scammer builds trust quickly with constant attention, then invents a crisis, a travel cost, or a can't-lose investment to extract money, gifts, or cryptocurrency. Some pivot to blackmail using intimate images. They almost always avoid meeting in person or on live video.
redFlags: A new online partner who quickly professes strong feelings
Excuses that prevent meeting in person or on live video
Requests for money, gift cards, or crypto for emergencies or travel
Being introduced to a 'great' investment or trading platform
Pressure to move to a private messaging app

faqs.question: Why won't they meet in person or on video?
faqs.answer: Scammers using a fake or stolen identity avoid live video and in-person meetings, offering constant excuses. A refusal to verify who they are is a major warning sign.

faqs.question: Is it safe to send money to an online partner?
faqs.answer: Be very cautious. Requests for money, gift cards, or crypto from someone you have only met online are a hallmark of romance scams, however genuine the relationship feels.

faqs.question: They introduced me to an investment. Is that normal?
faqs.answer: No. A new online partner steering you to a crypto or trading platform is a common romance-investment scam. Never invest on a partner's say-so.

howTheyWork: This is the slowest fraud there is. Weeks or months of daily messages come before any request, and by then the victim is defending the relationship to worried friends. The profile uses photographs taken from a real person, often a soldier, a doctor, an engineer or a widowed parent, with a job that explains being abroad. Conversation moves quickly from the dating app to a private messenger. The first ask is small and practical: a phone top-up, or a customs fee on a gift they say they posted to you. Larger ones follow a crisis.

Poor attempts declare love on day two in pasted paragraphs. Skilled ones remember your dog's name, your shift pattern, the anniversary of your husband's death. They send flowers. They mention money only when you raise it, and at first refuse help. Short video calls now happen, using face-swapping software, which weakens the old advice to insist on video. Requests come framed as loans with paperwork. Or they ask nothing for themselves and 'teach' you to invest on a site an uncle uses, so the affection and the theft seem unconnected.
whoIsTargeted: People newly alone after a divorce, a death, a move to a new town or retirement. Profiles that mention being widowed draw approaches within days. Members of faith-based and over-fifties dating sites are worked heavily, as are users of language-exchange and hobby apps that have nothing to do with dating. Contact intensifies around winter holidays, birthdays and anniversaries, when being alone weighs most.

firstSteps.title: Pause every payment, whatever the crisis
firstSteps.detail: Expect an emergency the moment you hesitate: a hospital bill, a seized passport, a threat to end things. Send nothing while you check, however unkind that feels.

firstSteps.title: Reverse-search their photographs
firstSteps.detail: Upload the profile pictures to an image search. The same face under a different name, or on a page warning about stolen photos, answers the question.

firstSteps.title: Show the messages to one person
firstSteps.detail: Let a friend or relative read the conversation today. Secrecy keeps this going, and an outside reader usually sees the pattern within minutes.

firstSteps.title: List past transfers for your bank
firstSteps.detail: Write down each payment with date and recipient, including gift cards and crypto. Ask the bank to investigate and to watch your account for unusual requests.

extraFaqs.question: We have had video calls. Can it still be a scam?
extraFaqs.answer: Yes. Live face-swapping tools let a scammer appear as the person in the photographs, and some groups pay models to take brief calls. Notice whether calls are always short or cut off 'because of the signal'. A video call shows you a face. It does not show a name, a location, or a reason this person needs your money.

extraFaqs.question: My parent is sending money to someone online and will not listen. What can I do?
extraFaqs.answer: Insisting the person is fake tends to deepen loyalty. Ask questions instead: have they met, what became of the last payment, would the partner join a video call with you present. Speak to the bank's fraud team, who can sometimes add safeguards with the customer's consent. Stay in touch, so there is somebody to turn to when doubt arrives.

name: Tech Support & Computer Scams
metaTitle: Tech Support & Computer Scams: Red Flags to Spot
metaDescription: Recognise tech support and computer scams: fake virus pop-ups, cold calls, remote access, refund tricks, and fake antivirus. See red flags and what to do.
summary: Tech support scams use fake virus warnings, pop-ups, and cold calls to gain remote access to your device, steal data, or trick you into bogus payments and refunds.
intro: Tech support and computer scams convince you that your device is infected, hacked, or compromised. They appear as alarming pop-ups, cold calls claiming to be from a well-known software company, or fake security alerts, and push you to call a number, install remote-access software, or pay for fake fixes and subscriptions. Once given access, scammers can view your screen, steal data, and manipulate your accounts.
redFlags: A pop-up or call claiming your device is infected or hacked
A request to install remote-access software
Pressure to pay for fixes, subscriptions, or refunds
A 'support' number from a pop-up, ad, or search result
Requests for passwords, card details, or remote control

faqs.question: Can a website or pop-up detect a virus on my device?
faqs.answer: No. A web page cannot scan your device. Pop-ups claiming you are infected and urging you to call a number are scams designed to scare you.

faqs.question: Should I let 'support' connect to my device?
faqs.answer: Only if you contacted a provider you trust through official channels. Granting remote access to an unsolicited caller lets scammers control your device and accounts.

faqs.question: How do I find genuine tech support?
faqs.answer: Use the official website or documentation for your device or software, not a number from a pop-up, ad, or search result.

howTheyWork: The aim is a remote session on your computer, with you watching and believing it is help. The way in is a full-screen browser page that refuses to close, flashing a virus warning with a siren and a phone number. Or a paid advert above the search results when you look up a printer maker's helpline. Or a cold call about 'errors your computer is sending us'. Once connected through an ordinary remote-desktop tool, the 'technician' opens harmless system logs, calls them infections, and sells a clean-up or a multi-year protection plan by card.

Clumsy operators just take the card payment. Polished ones run the refund trick. They log in to your online banking 'to return an overcharge', blank the screen, shift money between your own accounts so one balance jumps, and claim they refunded too much by mistake. You are asked to send back the difference by transfer, gift cards or cash in a parcel, and told the agent will be sacked otherwise. Nothing on screen is forged. The remote software is genuine and the log entries are real, which is why the whole thing feels technical and true.
whoIsTargeted: People comfortable enough with a computer to use it daily and not confident enough to diagnose it. Retired users feature heavily. Anyone searching for a support number in a hurry, such as when a printer fails before a deadline or a streaming stick will not activate. Mistyped web addresses and free film or download sites are where the locked-screen warnings usually appear.

firstSteps.title: Cut the internet connection
firstSteps.detail: Unplug the network cable or turn off wifi, then power the computer down. That ends the remote session even when the screen is locked or blank.

firstSteps.title: Phone the bank from another device
firstSteps.detail: Say a stranger had remote access while you were logged in to online banking. Ask for recent movements between your accounts to be checked and payments held.

firstSteps.title: Remove the remote-access program
firstSteps.detail: Restart offline and uninstall whatever was installed during the call. If you cannot tell which program it was, ask a local repair shop to check the machine.

firstSteps.title: Change passwords the browser had saved
firstSteps.detail: Assume everything stored in the browser was visible. From a clean device, change email and banking passwords first, then shopping and social accounts.

extraFaqs.question: A warning page has frozen my browser and will not close. What do I do?
extraFaqs.answer: It is only a web page. Do not ring the number. On a computer, close the browser with Task Manager on Windows or Force Quit on a Mac, then reopen it and decline to restore the previous tabs. On a phone, close the tab or clear the browser's data. Nothing was installed unless you agreed to a download.

extraFaqs.question: The technician says they refunded too much and wants it returned. Is that possible?
extraFaqs.answer: No refund was sent. While your screen was hidden they moved money from your savings to your current account, or edited the page so the balance looked higher. Whatever you 'return' is your own money leaving. Hang up, disconnect the computer, and phone your bank from a different device to hear your true balances.

name: Travel & Holiday Scams
metaTitle: Travel & Holiday Scams: Booking and Trip Red Flags
metaDescription: Spot travel and holiday scams: fake flights, hotels, holiday lets, visas, and package deals. See common red flags and how to book safely.
summary: Travel scams use fake flights, accommodation, packages, and visa services to take deposits and payments for trips that do not exist.
intro: Travel and holiday scams target people booking trips, using fake or copied listings, too-good-to-be-true package deals, and bogus visa or travel-authorisation services. Scammers take deposits or full payment by transfer for flights, hotels, or holiday lets that do not exist, or impersonate official visa sites to overcharge and harvest passport details. Many appear briefly through social media ads or unofficial websites.
redFlags: Prices far below normal for flights, hotels, or packages
Payment requested by bank transfer or gift card
Pressure to pay a deposit quickly to 'secure' a deal
Unofficial visa or travel-authorisation sites with high fees
Listings or agencies you cannot independently verify

faqs.question: How can I book travel safely?
faqs.answer: Use reputable, verifiable airlines, hotels, and platforms, pay by a method with protection, and confirm flights and hotels directly with the providers.

faqs.question: Why is a very cheap deal a warning sign?
faqs.answer: Prices far below normal, plus pressure to pay a deposit by transfer, are classic signs of a fake travel deal. Verify the seller before paying.

faqs.question: Where should I apply for a visa or travel authorisation?
faqs.answer: Only through the official government immigration website for your destination, found directly rather than via search ads charging inflated fees.

howTheyWork: Travel is bought months ahead and unseen, which gives a fraudster a long head start. You pay in spring for a villa in August, and nothing can be tested until you stand at the gate with luggage. The fake may be a listing, an 'agent' on social media, a cloned airline help desk or a visa site. Payment is steered to bank transfer with a discount for avoiding 'card fees'. You receive a booking reference, sometimes a genuine one that was reserved and never paid for, so it appears on the airline's site for a day and then lapses.

Obvious fakes offer a week in the sun at a price no operator could match. Credible ones sit only slightly under the market and blame a late cancellation. They send an itinerary with correct flight numbers and a contract to sign. Fake help desks are the sharpest form. You search for an airline's phone number after a cancelled flight, ring the advert at the top of the results, and a polite agent 'rebooks' you for a fee taken by card over the phone. The trip was real. The person who answered was not.
whoIsTargeted: Families booking school-holiday trips, when prices are highest and a bargain is most tempting. Pilgrims and festival-goers travelling on fixed dates with limited supply. Passengers stranded by strikes, storms or airline failures, who complain publicly and search frantically for a phone number. First-time visitors to a country that requires an electronic travel permit, who do not know what the official fee should be.

firstSteps.title: Verify the booking at source
firstSteps.detail: Enter your reference on the airline's or hotel's own site, or phone the property directly, and ask whether a paid reservation exists in your name.

firstSteps.title: Contact whoever moved the money
firstSteps.detail: Tell your card provider the travel was not supplied or the agent was fake. For a bank transfer, ask the bank to attempt an urgent recall.

firstSteps.title: Deal with passport details you uploaded
firstSteps.detail: If a fake visa site has your passport scan, inform your passport office, then reapply through the destination government's official channel so the trip can go ahead.

firstSteps.title: Check cover before rebooking
firstSteps.detail: Before buying replacement flights or rooms in a rush, ask your travel insurer what it covers, and whether the trade body the agent named has a claims process.

extraFaqs.question: My flight was cancelled and an account replied offering to rebook me. Is it the airline?
extraFaqs.answer: Check the handle character by character. Fake support accounts watch for complaints naming an airline and reply within minutes, asking you to DM a booking reference and phone number. A 'reservations desk' then calls and charges a rebooking fee. Airlines rebook through their app, their website, the airport desk or the number on your ticket confirmation.

extraFaqs.question: I arrived and the accommodation does not exist. What should I do first?
extraFaqs.answer: Find a safe place to sleep before anything else. Then gather evidence: photographs of the address, the listing, the messages and your payment record. Contact your card provider or bank that day, and the booking platform if you paid through one, since some help rehouse guests. Report it to local police if your insurer requires a crime reference.

name: Healthcare & Medical Scams
metaTitle: Healthcare & Medical Scams: Red Flags to Watch
metaDescription: Recognise healthcare and medical scams: fake insurance, pharmacies, miracle cures, medical devices, and patient-portal phishing. See red flags and safe steps.
summary: Healthcare scams exploit health worries with fake insurance, pharmacies, miracle cures, and medical-device offers, or phish your health and identity data.
intro: Healthcare and medical scams prey on health concerns and the cost of care. They include fake health insurance and discount plans, rogue online pharmacies, miracle cures and supplements, overpriced or fake medical devices, and phishing that impersonates patient portals, Medicare, or health agencies. Beyond financial loss, they risk your health and expose sensitive medical and identity data.
redFlags: Unsolicited offers of cheap insurance, medication, or cures
Miracle or guaranteed health claims
Requests for health, identity, or payment details
Pressure to enrol, buy, or verify immediately
Providers and pharmacies you cannot verify

faqs.question: How do I check a health provider or pharmacy is genuine?
faqs.answer: Verify it with your official health regulator or pharmacy register, and be wary of unsolicited offers, miracle claims, and prices that seem too good to be true.

faqs.question: Why are miracle cures a warning sign?
faqs.answer: Guaranteed cures and dramatic results are not how genuine medicine works. Such claims, often with free-trial billing traps, are a hallmark of health scams.

faqs.question: Is my health data valuable to scammers?
faqs.answer: Yes. Health and identity data can be used for fraud and identity theft, which is why many healthcare scams aim to collect it. Share it only through verified channels.

howTheyWork: Health fraud sells hope or sells cover, and occasionally sells nothing while collecting your details. The hope side is a product: pills, patches, drops or gadgets advertised with before-and-after photographs and a doctor in a white coat who may be an actor or a generated face. The cover side is a phone call offering a cheap plan, a back brace, a genetic test or an alarm pendant 'already paid for', which requires your insurance or health service number to 'confirm eligibility'. That number is then used to bill for equipment and tests you never receive.

Crude adverts promise to melt fat overnight. Better operations borrow legitimacy. They run pages styled like a health magazine article, drop a real university's name, and show a pharmacy seal that links nowhere. Rogue pharmacies ask a few questions on a web form and call it a consultation, then ship tablets of unknown content in plausible blister packs. Callers already hold your name, age and condition from a lead form you once completed for a quote, and say your own doctor referred you.
whoIsTargeted: People managing long-term conditions such as diabetes, arthritis or chronic pain, and those facing a frightening diagnosis who search for alternatives at night. Anyone priced out of a prescription. Older adults during insurance enrolment periods, when calls about switching plans are expected. People too embarrassed to see a doctor about weight, hair loss or sexual health, who would sooner order privately.

firstSteps.title: Stop using the product
firstSteps.detail: If tablets or drops arrived from an unverified seller, take no more. Keep the packaging and ask a pharmacist or doctor about anything you have already swallowed.

firstSteps.title: Shut off the repeat billing
firstSteps.detail: 'Free sample' health offers usually enrol you in repeat deliveries. Ask your card provider to block future payments to the merchant and dispute those already taken.

firstSteps.title: Read your next benefits statement
firstSteps.detail: If you gave a policy or health service number, look for equipment, tests or appointments you never had, and report each one to the insurer or programme.

firstSteps.title: Tell your own clinician
firstSteps.detail: Let your GP or specialist know what you were sold and which details you shared, so false entries do not end up shaping your medical record.

extraFaqs.question: I gave my insurance number for a 'free' medical device. What happens now?
