extraFaqs.answer: The caller's company may bill your insurer or health programme for braces, test kits or equipment in your name. That can use up an allowance you need later and leave false conditions on file. Phone the fraud line of your insurer or programme, ask for recent claims to be reviewed, and refuse parcels you did not order, noting the sender.

extraFaqs.question: Is medicine bought from an unverified website dangerous to take?
extraFaqs.answer: Sometimes, yes. Tablets from unregistered sellers have turned up with the wrong dose, a different drug, or no active ingredient, and nobody has checked them against your other medicines. If you have taken some and feel unwell, seek medical help and bring the packaging. Otherwise stop, and ask a pharmacist how to get a safe supply.

name: Identity Theft & Data Scams
metaTitle: Identity Theft & Data Scams: Red Flags and Steps
metaDescription: Recognise identity theft and data scams: account takeover, SIM swap, data breaches, synthetic identity, and document fraud. See red flags and how to respond.
summary: Identity theft scams steal your personal data and credentials to take over accounts, open credit, or impersonate you, often after phishing or data breaches.
intro: Identity theft and data scams aim to capture the personal information and credentials needed to impersonate you. They follow on from phishing, data breaches, SIM swaps, and account takeovers, and can be used to open accounts or credit in your name, drain existing accounts, or commit fraud that lands at your door. Spotting the early signs and locking down your accounts quickly limits the damage.
redFlags: Unexpected verification codes, password resets, or account changes
Bills, accounts, or credit applications you did not make
Losing mobile signal suddenly, a possible SIM swap
Mail or statements stopping or going missing
Notices that your data appeared in a breach

faqs.question: What should I do first if I suspect identity theft?
faqs.answer: Secure your email and key accounts with new passwords and two-factor authentication, contact your bank, check your credit report, and report it to your fraud authority.

faqs.question: How do scammers get my details?
faqs.answer: Through phishing, data breaches, SIM swaps, mail theft, and account takeovers. Strong, unique passwords and two-factor authentication make misuse much harder.

faqs.question: What is a SIM swap?
faqs.answer: It is when a scammer takes control of your phone number to intercept codes and calls. A sudden loss of mobile signal can be a sign; contact your carrier immediately.

howTheyWork: An identity is assembled piece by piece, seldom grabbed in one go. A name and date of birth from one breach, an address from a public register, a mother's maiden name from a social media quiz, a password from an old forum leak. The pieces are traded and combined until there is enough to answer a call centre's security questions or pass an online credit application. Often nobody contacts you at all. When they do, it is a 'verification' form, a fake breach notice asking you to confirm details, or a call to your mobile network pretending to be you.

Clumsy fraud surfaces fast, as when a card you never ordered arrives at your own address. Careful fraud hides. The thief redirects your post, switches statements to paperless, and adds an email address of their own so alerts go elsewhere. They open one small account and run it well for months to build a record before borrowing heavily. A child's identity is prized for the same reason, since nobody looks at a ten-year-old's credit file. The first sign may be a debt collector's letter, or a mortgage application turned down.
whoIsTargeted: People whose details sat in a breached database, which by now means most adults. Risk climbs when paperwork is in motion: after a house move, while post still goes to the old flat; after a death, when the accounts of the deceased lie unwatched; after a lost wallet or stolen phone. Children, and students sharing a communal letterbox, are found out last.

firstSteps.title: Lock your email and mobile account
firstSteps.detail: Change the email password, turn on app-based two-step sign-in, and ask your mobile network whether it can add a PIN required before any SIM change.

firstSteps.title: Order your credit reports
firstSteps.detail: Request your file from each credit reference agency and mark every account, search and address you do not recognise. Each needs disputing with the lender named.

firstSteps.title: Set a freeze or protective marker
firstSteps.detail: Where a credit freeze exists, place one with every agency. Elsewhere, ask about a protective registration so that lenders carry out extra checks on applications.

firstSteps.title: Keep a dated log
firstSteps.detail: Record each call with the date, organisation, person and reference number. Clearing this up takes weeks, and lenders and police ask for the same facts repeatedly.

extraFaqs.question: Does a credit freeze stop my existing cards and accounts from working?
extraFaqs.answer: It does not. A freeze prevents new lenders from pulling your file, which blocks most fresh applications in your name. Cards, loans and accounts you already hold carry on as before. When you want credit yourself, you lift the freeze for a while using a PIN or login, then restore it. Availability and method differ between countries.

extraFaqs.question: Why would anyone steal a child's identity?
extraFaqs.answer: A child has a clean record and nobody watching it. An identity number paired with a false date of birth can open accounts that run unnoticed for years, until the child applies for a first card or a student loan. Warning signs include letters from lenders addressed to the child, or a credit file existing at all for someone that young.

name: Small Business & Workplace Scams
metaTitle: Small Business & Workplace Scams: Red Flags
metaDescription: Recognise scams targeting businesses: fake invoices, CEO fraud, supplier and mandate fraud, directory listings, and domain or SEO cons. See red flags and steps.
summary: Business scams target companies and employees with fake invoices, CEO and supplier fraud, bogus directory and domain bills, and payroll diversion.
intro: Small business and workplace scams target organisations and their staff. They include fake invoices and supplier mandate changes, CEO and business email compromise, bogus directory or trademark listings, domain and SEO cons, payroll diversion, and fake utility or equipment bills. They rely on busy teams, authority, and routine payment processes to slip through, often costing far more than consumer scams.
redFlags: An unexpected change to a supplier's bank details
Urgent payment or gift card requests from a 'boss'
Invoices or bills for services you did not order
Pressure that bypasses normal approval processes
Look-alike sender addresses and domains

faqs.question: How do we prevent invoice and mandate fraud?
faqs.answer: Verify any change to a supplier's bank details by phone using a known number, require dual approval for payments, and be alert to look-alike email addresses.

faqs.question: Why are gift card requests from a 'boss' a red flag?
faqs.answer: Gift card codes are fast and hard to trace, so scammers favour them in CEO fraud. Verify any unusual request in person or on a known number before acting.

faqs.question: Are directory and domain bills genuine?
faqs.answer: Many unsolicited directory, domain, or trademark 'renewal' notices are bogus. Check against your real records and verify the provider before paying.

howTheyWork: Companies pay strangers every day on the strength of a document, and that habit is the opening. An invoice arrives, it resembles hundreds of others, somebody keys it in. Business fraud inserts itself into that flow. An email from a supplier's address, or one a single character off, gives new bank details for future payments. A message from the managing director asks finance for an urgent, confidential transfer. A member of staff appears to email HR with a new salary account. Each payment is approved by a real employee following something close to normal procedure.

Low-effort attempts are bulk mailings: an official-looking demand to renew a trademark or a directory entry, counting on a junior paying it unread. Targeted ones begin with reading. The criminal sits inside a compromised mailbox for weeks, learning who approves payments, when the director travels and how invoices are worded, then acts when a large one falls due. The change-of-details letter carries the right logo, the right contact's signature and a reason, such as an audit. A follow-up call 'from the supplier' confirms it, on a number supplied in the fraudulent email.
whoIsTargeted: Accounts payable clerks, payroll administrators, executive assistants and office managers: whoever can move money or amend a record. Newly registered companies, whose details sit on public registers and attract fake compliance bills within weeks. Firms midway through a property deal, an acquisition or a large supply contract. Financial year end, holiday cover and the director's week abroad are favoured moments.

firstSteps.title: Ring the bank's business fraud line
firstSteps.detail: Give the payment reference, amount and beneficiary details and request an immediate recall. Speed counts for more here than a complete account of what happened.

firstSteps.title: Speak to the real supplier or director
firstSteps.detail: Use the number in your existing records, never the one in the email. Work out whether their mailbox or yours is the compromised one.

firstSteps.title: Secure the affected mailbox
firstSteps.detail: Have IT reset the password, end active sessions and search for inbox rules that hide or forward messages containing words such as 'invoice' or 'payment'.

firstSteps.title: Suspend changes to payee records
firstSteps.detail: Hold all bank-detail amendments and new payees until every recent change has been confirmed by phone with a contact you already know.

extraFaqs.question: The request came from our director's real email address. How is that possible?
extraFaqs.answer: Either the director's mailbox has been broken into, usually through a phished password, or the display name is right and the underlying address is not. Mobile mail apps often show only the name. Open the full address and look at the reply-to field, which is frequently set to an outside account. Confirm any payment request by phone or in person.

extraFaqs.question: An employee emailed asking to change their salary bank account. How should we check?
extraFaqs.answer: Treat it like a supplier change and never act on the email alone. Speak to the employee face to face, or call the number already on file, and have them make the change themselves in the payroll system where one exists. These requests tend to arrive a few days before the pay run, leaving little room to query them.

name: Gaming & In-App Scams
metaTitle: Gaming & In-App Scams: Red Flags for Players
metaDescription: Recognise gaming and in-app scams: free currency generators, account trades, phishing, fake skins, and in-game purchase fraud. See red flags and safe steps.
summary: Gaming scams target players with fake free-currency offers, account trades, phishing links, and in-game item fraud that steal logins, money, or accounts.
intro: Gaming and in-app scams target players, often younger ones, through free-currency or skin 'generators', account buying and trading, phishing links in chats and Discord servers, fake giveaways, and in-app purchase fraud. They aim to steal account logins, payment details, or valuable in-game items, and frequently use the promise of free rewards and urgency to lower players' guard.
redFlags: Offers of free in-game currency, skins, or items
A request to log in via a link or share your account
Account buying, selling, or 'boosting' from strangers
Fake giveaways requiring a fee or your login
Pressure to act fast before an offer expires

faqs.question: Are free currency or skin generators real?
faqs.answer: No. 'Generators' for free in-game currency or items are scams that steal logins or push surveys and malware. Genuine currency is bought through official stores.

faqs.question: Is it safe to buy or sell game accounts?
faqs.answer: It is risky and often against the rules. Buyers can be scammed and accounts reclaimed, and sharing logins can lead to takeover. Avoid account trading with strangers.

faqs.question: How do I protect my gaming account?
faqs.answer: Use a strong unique password, enable two-factor authentication, and never log in through links in chats, DMs, or 'giveaway' pages.

howTheyWork: Game accounts hold things with resale value: rare skins, ranked progress, currency bought with real money, a library of purchased titles. Thieves want the login, and they get it with a link. A message in the platform's chat or on a voice server says a friend has gifted you a subscription, asks you to vote for their team, or claims you have been reported. The page behind it copies the platform's sign-in window, including a prompt for the code from your authenticator. Within minutes the inventory is traded to a holding account and sold for cash on an outside site.

Generator sites promising unlimited currency for completing offers fool mainly younger players. Sharper tricks are aimed at experienced traders. A middleman 'trusted by the community' holds both items during a swap and disappears. A buyer pays by a method that can be reversed once the item has moved. Someone with a staff-style avatar and name says your account is flagged and asks you to transfer items to a 'verification' account. Malware arrives as a cheat, a mod, or 'a game I am developing, can you test it', and steals the browser's saved sessions.
whoIsTargeted: Children and teenagers, who own accounts of real value, have little experience of fraud, and sometimes play with a parent's card saved on the console. Players of games with tradeable items and busy outside marketplaces. Streamers, whose usernames are public and whose viewers can be reached with fake giveaways. Attempts jump at season launches, big updates and school holidays.

firstSteps.title: Reset password and authenticator
firstSteps.detail: Change the account password, re-register your authenticator, and revoke any API key or trade link, because thieves use those to redirect future trades.

firstSteps.title: Deauthorise every other device
firstSteps.detail: Use the platform's option to sign out everywhere. A stolen session token goes on working after a password change until all devices are logged out.

firstSteps.title: Open a ticket with official support
firstSteps.detail: Give the account name, the original email, purchase receipts and the time things changed. Proof of the first purchase is what support staff most often request.

firstSteps.title: Inspect the saved payment card
firstSteps.detail: Look through purchase history for currency or gifts you did not buy, remove the card from the account, and tell the card provider about unfamiliar charges.

extraFaqs.question: Can a stolen skin or item be put back in my account?
extraFaqs.answer: Policies differ between publishers. Many will not restore items that left through a completed trade, because duplicating them affects other players, though some roll an account back after a proven takeover. Report quickly to official support with evidence and ask what applies. Be wary of anyone on a forum who claims to retrieve items for a fee.

extraFaqs.question: My child spent money in a game after talking to a stranger. What now?
extraFaqs.answer: Stay calm with them, because children who fear punishment hide the next incident. Save the chat, report the other player inside the game, and find out which card or gift balance was used. Ask the platform and your card provider about the charges. Then switch on purchase approval and spending limits in the console's or app store's family settings.

name: AI & Deepfake Scams
metaTitle: AI & Deepfake Scams: Voice and Video Red Flags
metaDescription: Recognise AI and deepfake scams: cloned voices, fake celebrity videos, AI investment bots, and synthetic identities. See red flags and how to verify.
summary: AI scams use cloned voices, deepfake videos, and synthetic identities to impersonate people you trust and lend false credibility to fraud.
intro: AI and deepfake scams use generated voices, faces, and text to make fraud more convincing. They include cloned voices imitating a relative in distress, deepfake videos of celebrities or officials endorsing schemes, AI 'trading bots' promising guaranteed returns, and synthetic identities built to pass checks. The defence is the same as ever: slow down, verify through trusted channels, and treat urgency and too-good-to-be-true offers with caution.
redFlags: A 'relative' in urgent trouble whose voice sounds slightly off
A celebrity or official video endorsing a money-making scheme
Pressure to act before you can verify
An AI bot or platform promising guaranteed returns
Requests for money, codes, or details based on a call or video alone

faqs.question: Can scammers really clone a voice?
faqs.answer: Yes. With a short audio sample, AI can imitate someone's voice. If a 'relative' calls in urgent trouble, verify by calling them back on their known number and ask a question only they would know.

faqs.question: How do I spot a deepfake video?
faqs.answer: Look for odd lighting, glitches, or lip-sync issues, and be sceptical of celebrities or officials endorsing money-making schemes. Always verify through official, verified channels.

faqs.question: Are AI trading bots legitimate?
faqs.answer: Promises of guaranteed returns from an 'AI bot' are a hallmark of investment fraud. No bot can guarantee profits, and many are simply a front for a scam platform.

howTheyWork: Generated media changes one thing about fraud: the proof. A voice on the phone, a face on a video call, a clip of a public figure speaking, all used to count as evidence that someone was who they claimed to be. A short sample of speech from a public video is enough to build a voice that will read any script. Face-swap software runs live on an ordinary laptop. The frauds underneath are old ones, the emergency call from a child, the boss ordering a transfer, the famous investor recommending a platform, with the doubt removed by something you saw or heard.

Weak fakes are caught by eye and ear: lips drifting off the words, a flat stare, a voice with no breath in it. Strong ones avoid scrutiny by design. The cloned voice speaks for ten seconds, sobbing, then hands over to a 'police officer' or 'kidnapper' who is a live person. The deepfake director appears in a group video meeting beside other fabricated colleagues, on a poor connection, camera on briefly. Celebrity clips are cut short, subtitled, and run as adverts for a day before removal. The quality only has to survive a few seconds of shock.
whoIsTargeted: Parents and grandparents of anyone with video or voice clips online, which now covers most teenagers. Finance staff at companies whose executives give interviews and conference talks. Followers of well-known investors, presenters and doctors, whose faces are borrowed for adverts. People seeking company from chatbot 'partners', who are gradually steered towards paid upgrades, gifts or a recommended investment.

firstSteps.title: Ring the real person yourself
firstSteps.detail: Hang up and call your relative or colleague on the number you already hold. If there is no answer, try someone who is physically with them.

firstSteps.title: Ask something no script contains
firstSteps.detail: If the call continues, ask for a detail that has never been online: a childhood nickname, what you ate together last Sunday. A cloned voice cannot improvise memory.

firstSteps.title: Recall any payment already sent
firstSteps.detail: If a transfer was made on the strength of the call or video, phone your bank immediately and explain that you were deceived by an impersonation.

firstSteps.title: Preserve the recording or advert
firstSteps.detail: Save the voicemail, the meeting link or the advert's address. Platforms and investigators need the original, and fake adverts are frequently deleted within hours.

extraFaqs.question: Should my family agree a safe word for emergency calls?
extraFaqs.answer: It is one of the few defences that does not rely on spotting flaws. Choose a word or phrase that has never appeared online, agree it face to face, and use it only when someone asks for money or says they are in danger. Tell children and grandparents alike. A caller who cannot give it gets a call back on the usual number.

extraFaqs.question: Should I stop posting videos of myself to avoid voice cloning?
extraFaqs.answer: You can reduce what is public, though for most people some audio already exists and cannot be recalled. Private profiles limit who can copy your voice and who can map your family connections, which the script depends on. The stronger protection sits at the receiving end: relatives who know that a familiar voice asking for money still needs checking.

name: Utility & Energy Scams
metaTitle: Utility & Energy Scams: Bill and Refund Red Flags
metaDescription: Recognise utility and energy scams: fake disconnection threats, refunds, meter and grant cons, and supplier impersonation. See red flags and how to check.
summary: Utility scams impersonate energy, water, and broadband providers with fake bills, refunds, disconnection threats, and grant or meter cons.
intro: Utility and energy scams impersonate your electricity, gas, water, or broadband provider. They use fake overdue bills, refund or rebate lures, disconnection threats, and bogus grant, meter, or efficiency schemes to collect payments and card or account details, or to gain access to your home. They often spike when energy costs rise and people are anxious about bills.
redFlags: A bill, refund, or disconnection threat demanding urgent payment
A link to pay or confirm details outside your provider's app
Unsolicited 'grant', meter, or efficiency offers
Callers or visitors pressuring you about your supply
Requests for card or account details to avoid a cut-off

faqs.question: Can my utility supply be cut off without warning?
faqs.answer: Genuine suppliers handle arrears through proper notices and your account, not urgent calls or texts demanding instant payment to avoid disconnection. Verify any threat with your provider directly.

faqs.question: How do I check a utility refund or grant is real?
faqs.answer: Log in to your provider's official app or website, or call the number on a genuine bill. Never confirm card details or pay via a link in an unexpected message.

faqs.question: Someone came to my door about my meter or energy. Is it safe?
faqs.answer: Ask for identification, do not feel pressured, and verify with your supplier using official contacts before allowing access or agreeing to anything.

howTheyWork: Utilities are the one bill nobody can ignore, since losing power, heat or water is an immediate problem. The fraud takes two routes. By phone or text, a 'disconnection team' says your account is in arrears and a crew is booked for this afternoon unless you pay now, by card or with a prepaid voucher. At the door, someone in a hi-vis jacket and lanyard needs to read the meter, test water pressure after 'works in the street', or assess you for a grant, and either takes a deposit or keeps you talking while a partner searches the house.

A crude caller cannot say which company supplies you. A prepared one names your supplier, your tariff and roughly what you owe, picked up from a comparison-site form or an earlier doorstep 'survey'. Refund emails match a real billing cycle and use the supplier's template. Grant offers convince because real schemes exist: governments do fund insulation and boiler replacement, so a salesperson citing a genuine scheme name and asking for a 'survey fee' sounds routine. Doorstep sellers of cut-price prepayment credit complete the set, offering top-ups the supplier never receives payment for.
whoIsTargeted: Households on prepayment meters, and small shops and cafes that cannot trade without power. Tenants who have just moved in and are unsure which company supplies the address. Older homeowners, approached at the door about grants and meter replacements. Calls and texts rise in winter, after price announcements, and following storms or street works, when a visit from an engineer seems expected.

firstSteps.title: Ask the supplier what is recorded
firstSteps.detail: Log in to your account or ring the number on a paper bill. Ask whether any arrears, disconnection notice, refund or engineer visit is recorded for your address.

firstSteps.title: Chase the card or voucher payment
firstSteps.detail: If you paid by card, call the issuer. If you read out a prepaid voucher code, contact the voucher company at once with the receipt in hand.

firstSteps.title: Check rooms after a doorstep visit
firstSteps.detail: If someone came inside, look through bedrooms and drawers for missing cash, jewellery and bank cards, and call the police non-emergency line whatever you find.

firstSteps.title: Cancel what you signed at the door
firstSteps.detail: If you agreed to switch supplier or ordered insulation or a boiler, write to cancel immediately. Many countries give a cooling-off period for doorstep sales.

extraFaqs.question: I bought cheap meter top-up credit from someone at the door. Will it work?
extraFaqs.answer: It may register as credit for a while, but credit sold outside official outlets has not been paid for with your supplier. When the supplier notices the gap, it can bill you for the energy used, so you pay twice. Buy credit only through the supplier's app or website or at a registered shop terminal, and tell the supplier about any doorstep top-up.

extraFaqs.question: Can an energy company switch my supply without my agreement?
extraFaqs.answer: A switch without consent should not happen, yet it does, through a doorstep seller or caller who records a 'yes' to a vague question or forges a signature. The usual sign is a welcome letter from a company you never chose, or a final bill from your own supplier. Contact both, say you gave no consent, and ask to be returned to your original tariff.
